passage:
In the inter-school camp dining hall, a parent volunteer stopped Noor at the long table. 'Beta, you sit at that side table. These children are from pure-veg families.' Noor was holding the same dal and rice as everyone else. Noor's face burned.
Akash, who had been saving the seat, stood up. 'She's eating exactly what we're eating.'
'Rules are rules,' the volunteer said. Noor went to the side table anyway, head down.
Akash went straight to Mrs. Pillai, the camp teacher. Within ten minutes she was in the hall. She told the volunteer clearly, 'Nobody at this camp eats apart because of their religion. That is exclusion, and it stops now.' Then she carried her own plate to the side table, sat beside Noor, and asked Akash to bring the others over.

qa.q: Who did Akash go to for help?
qa.a: Mrs. Pillai, the camp teacher.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when told to sit at the side table?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and hurt, her face burning, made to feel less than the others even though her plate was the same.

qa.q: What did Mrs. Pillai do that others could learn from?
qa.a: She came the same day, named the separate seating as exclusion, stopped it, and sat with Noor herself so Noor was not alone.

qa.q: How might the parent volunteer see things after Mrs. Pillai's words?
qa.a: The volunteer may feel embarrassed or defensive at first, but has been told clearly that separating a child by religion is wrong.

grounding: Shows a teenager told to eat apart because of religion, the hurt it causes, and an adult who names the exclusion as wrong and ends it.

passage:
Dear Ujjwal Bhaiya,
Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. Nisha's family had a lunch after their griha pravesh, and our whole class group was invited except me. Nisha told me quietly that her Dadi had said 'our kind only' in the kitchen. I laughed like it didn't matter. Then I cried in the bus.
That evening I told Papa. He put down his tea and said, 'Rashmi, this is caste, and it is wrong. It is not about you.' He called Nisha's mother that same night, calmly. She was shocked; she hadn't known about the list. Today Nisha came to school with sweets from the puja and said her mother is talking to her Dadi. I don't know if I'll go next time. But I felt heard.
Rashmi

qa.q: What did Nisha's Dadi say in the kitchen?
qa.a: 'Our kind only.'

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling after hearing why the invitation never came?
qa.a: Rashmi felt deeply hurt and humiliated, laughing it off in front of Nisha but crying in the bus.

qa.q: What did Papa do right when Rashmi told him?
qa.a: He named it as caste and wrong, told Rashmi it was not about Rashmi, and called Nisha's mother calmly that same night.

qa.q: How might Nisha feel about what her Dadi did?
qa.a: Nisha seems uncomfortable and sorry, which is why Nisha told Rashmi quietly and later brought sweets.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager left out of a meal because of caste, the deep hurt it brings, and adults who name the exclusion as wrong and act to end it.

passage:
The only dhaba near the college in Sagar had four plastic tables, and Farhan's group took two every evening. Farhan, nineteen, always ordered first for Parul: plain dal, no onion, no garlic, roti kept away from the non-veg pan. He had learnt her Jain rules in the first week and never joked about them. His own Ammi's rule was halal only, so he stuck to paneer here.
One evening Deepak pulled his chair back when Ramu, the cleaner's son who studied with them, sat down. 'My family doesn't eat with—'
Farhan cut in, quietly. 'Parul's rule is about what's on her plate. Yours is about a person. That's different.'
Parul nodded and passed Ramu the pickle. Deepak looked away, but stayed.

qa.q: What did Farhan order for Parul?
qa.a: Plain dal, no onion, no garlic, and roti kept away from the non-veg pan.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when Deepak pulled his chair back from Ramu?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and quietly angry at the unfairness, yet calm enough to speak without shaming Deepak loudly.

qa.q: How did Farhan balance respect for food rules with fairness?
qa.a: He respected Parul's diet and his own family's rule, but pointed out that refusing to eat with a person is different and unfair.

qa.q: How might Ramu have felt when Parul passed him the pickle?
qa.a: Ramu probably felt accepted and relieved, seeing friends stand by him instead of letting Deepak's rule push him away.

grounding: Shows a young adult at college who shares meals across faiths and diets, respects a friend's food restrictions, and questions an unfair idea about who may eat together.

passage:
In the shared kitchen of their residence in Cape Town, Diego, twenty, was making his grandmother's pozole for Sunday dinner, the way his family did every week back in Monterrey. Pork, of course. Then he remembered: Aisha ate halal, and Kiran was vegetarian. He split the pot, made a bean version on the side, and labelled both.
When Thabo came in to help, Lars muttered that Thabo's pan was 'dirty' because tripe had been cooked in it. Diego frowned. 'It's washed. If you don't eat tripe, fine. But a pan isn't dirty because of who used it.' Thabo shrugged, jaw tight.
That night eight people ate from two pots, and Diego handed Thabo the first bowl.

qa.q: Which dish was Diego making?
qa.a: His grandmother's pozole.

qa.q: What was Diego feeling when Lars called Thabo's pan dirty?
qa.a: Diego felt uncomfortable and annoyed at the unfairness, frowning because the remark was really about a person, not the food.

qa.q: What did Diego do well to respect everyone at the table?
qa.a: He split the pot into a pork and a bean version with labels so Aisha and Kiran could eat, and challenged the unfair remark about Thabo.

qa.q: How might Thabo have felt when Diego defended the pan and served Thabo first?
qa.a: Thabo probably felt respected and less alone after the hurtful remark, though the tight jaw shows it still stung.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult in a student residence who shares meals across faiths and diets, respecting friends' restrictions while questioning an unfair purity idea.

passage: Noor, you asked why my kitchen has two tiffin boxes. Let your old Hansa Ba tell you. When I was twenty-four and newly running my own house in Ahmedabad, we were strict Jain: no onion, no garlic, nothing after sunset. My husband's colleague, Mr. Fernandes, was coming to dinner with his wife, and I panicked. Would they find our food bland? My mother-in-law said, 'Serve what we eat, and they'll learn.' Instead I cooked our dal as always, bought a small tin of fried onions from the market, set it on a separate plate at their places, and said, 'Please, as you like.' Mrs. Fernandes cried, 'You thought of us!' We ate together for forty years after that. My food stayed mine. My table became everyone's.

qa.q: Where was Hansa running her own house at twenty-four?
qa.a: In Ahmedabad.

qa.q: What was young Hansa feeling before the Fernandes dinner?
qa.a: She felt panicked and anxious that the guests would find her Jain food bland.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the dinner work, and why?
qa.a: Hansa kept her own dal but set fried onions on a separate plate for the guests, so she honoured her custom and still gave them a choice.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Fernandes experience Hansa's gesture?
qa.a: She felt touched and cared for, crying, 'You thought of us!', which began a forty-year friendship.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps her family's food custom at home yet offers guests a choice and never mocks their plate, so tradition does not become a wall.

passage: Saga Dawa month meant no meat in Tenzin's kitchen, the way it had been in Ama's house in Dharamshala. But tonight six friends were coming, Simran among them, the one who called any meal without chicken 'just a snack'. Then the rain knocked out the power, leaving one gas burner and a torch. Tenzin, twenty-five, made a big pot of vegetable thenthuk and, with the last of the phone battery, ordered a plate of chicken momos from the corner shop for anyone who wanted them, kept on a separate plate by the door. Simran arrived dripping, laughed at the torchlight, then went back for the thenthuk twice. 'Okay, this is not a snack.' Nobody teased anyone's plate. The momos disappeared too.

qa.q: What did Tenzin cook in the big pot?
qa.a: Vegetable thenthuk.

qa.q: What was Tenzin probably feeling when the power went out with six friends on the way?
qa.a: Tenzin was probably worried and under pressure, with one burner, a torch and guests coming, yet calm enough to plan.

qa.q: How did Tenzin keep the custom and still welcome everyone, despite the power cut?
qa.a: Tenzin kept the kitchen meat-free but offered chicken momos from outside on a separate plate, and nobody mocked anyone's choice.

qa.q: How did Simran's view of a meatless meal change?
qa.a: Simran moved from calling it 'just a snack' to going back twice and saying so, because it was offered warmly, without a lecture.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who keeps a family food custom at home while offering guests a choice and never mocking anyone's plate.

passage:
At Amara's flat in London, Nadia watched Amara's mother arrive from Lagos with three coolers of food. By the second evening, Mrs. Okafor had filled Amara's plate with jollof rice four times. When Amara said, 'Mummy, I'm full,' her mother's smile fell. 'You don't like my cooking anymore?' She turned back to the stove, shoulders stiff.
Nadia saw Amara pause, then go over and hug her mother from behind. 'I love it so much I want it for breakfast too. Pack me some for tomorrow?'
Her mother laughed and took the plate. Nadia, whose own mother did the same with parathas, understood. The food was never really about hunger.

qa.q: Where had Amara's mother come from?
qa.a: From Lagos.

qa.q: What did Nadia feel watching this, and why?
qa.a: Nadia felt understanding and fondness, recognising her own mother's parathas in Mrs. Okafor's jollof rice.

qa.q: What made Amara's second reply work?
qa.a: Amara hugged her mother, praised the food and asked for some for breakfast, accepting the love without eating past fullness.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Okafor seem to take Amara's first 'I'm full'?
qa.a: She seemed hurt and rejected, as if Amara no longer liked her cooking, which is why her smile fell and her shoulders stiffened.

grounding: Shows an observer who sees that a mother's piling of food is her language of love, and a kind response that thanks her warmly instead of simply refusing.

passage:
On visiting Sunday at the working women's hostel in Pune, Sarita watched her roommate Kiran's Amma unpack a steel tiffin carrier in the common room. Roti after roti landed on Kiran's plate.
'Amma, enough, three is plenty.'
Amma's hand froze in the air, the fourth roti hanging. 'You don't want my food now?'
Kiran took a breath, took the roti, and broke it in half. 'I'll eat this half now and the rest at dinner, so I can think of you tonight.'
Amma's face softened. Sarita noticed she still tucked two more rotis into Kiran's cupboard before leaving.

qa.q: How many rotis did Kiran say were plenty?
qa.a: Three is plenty.

qa.q: What might Sarita have felt watching Amma tuck extra rotis into the cupboard?
qa.a: Sarita likely felt amused and touched, seeing how Amma's love kept finding a way through food.

qa.q: What was kind about Kiran's response?
qa.a: Kiran accepted the roti, ate a little and explained warmly that the rest would help Kiran think of Amma, so the love was received.

qa.q: How did Amma seem to feel when Kiran said 'enough'?
qa.a: Amma seemed hurt and worried, taking the refusal as a rejection of her love, which is why her hand froze.

grounding: Illustrates an observer seeing a mother keep piling roti on a plate and take refusal as rejection, and a warm response that accepts a little and explains kindly.

passage: On Diwali night in the village, two-year-old Anjali sat on the courtyard wall in her new red frock, staring at the rows of clay diyas and patting the air toward them. Nana gave her a piece of barfi; she smeared it on her cheek, delighted. A cracker boomed near the well. Anjali screamed, burying her face in Nana's kurta. Their neighbour Rafiq cupped his hands over her ears, and soon she peeked out at the lights again.

qa.q: What was Anjali wearing?
qa.a: Her new red frock.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when the cracker boomed?
qa.a: She felt frightened by the loud noise, screaming and hiding her face in Nana's kurta.

qa.q: How can adults help a toddler like Anjali enjoy a noisy festival?
qa.a: Keep her away from crackers, cover her ears and hold her close, so she can keep watching the lights safely.

qa.q: How might Nana feel with Anjali clinging to him after the boom?
qa.a: Nana probably feels protective and tender, glad to be her safe place in the noise.

grounding: Shows a toddler at Diwali who reacts to lamps and sweets with wonder and to a loud cracker with fear, absorbing the festive mood without knowing its meaning.

passage: At the Christmas market in Sapporo, Hiroshi carried eighteen-month-old Hana, snug in a new white snowsuit, toward the giant tree. Her mouth fell open at the blinking gold lights. She stretched both mittens toward them and squealed. Then a brass band struck up right beside them. Hana's face crumpled and she buried it in Hiroshi's scarf. He walked a little way off, humming, until she lifted her head to stare at the lights again.

qa.q: What colour was Hana's new snowsuit?
qa.a: White.

qa.q: How did Hana feel when she saw the blinking gold lights?
qa.a: She felt amazed and delighted, mouth open, reaching toward them and squealing.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi do that helped Hana when the band started?
qa.a: He moved a little way from the noise and hummed, so she felt safe enough to look at the lights again.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi feel watching Hana's wonder at the tree?
qa.a: Hiroshi likely feels joyful and tender, sharing in her delight at the festival lights.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler at a Christmas market who meets the lights with wonder and the loud music with fear, taking in the festive mood without knowing its meaning.

passage: Early on Gudi Padwa morning, Mahima Tai swept the yard in front of the village house and handed five-year-old Tushar a small bowl of orange colour. 'Your job: fill every petal on this side.' Tushar crouched, tongue between his teeth, and pinched the colour out slowly. Some fell outside the lines. Mahima Tai didn't fix it. When the neighbours came to look, Tushar stood by his side of the rangoli with orange fingers and announced, 'I made this part.' That night he asked, 'When's the next festival?'

qa.q: What did Mahima Tai hand Tushar?
qa.a: A small bowl of orange colour.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he announced, 'I made this part'?
qa.a: He felt proud and important, having done a real job for the festival.

qa.q: What did Mahima Tai get right in giving Tushar the task?
qa.a: She gave him a clear, real job and didn't fix his mistakes, so that part of the rangoli truly felt like his.

qa.q: How might Mahima Tai feel hearing Tushar ask, 'When's the next festival?'
qa.a: She would likely feel happy and amused, seeing that he now looks forward to festivals.

grounding: Shows a young child given a real part in making a festival rangoli, who is proud of the task and starts looking forward to the next festival.

passage: The week before Lunar New Year, Mr. Chen from the bakery downstairs asked five-year-old Beatriz if she could help. 'Very important job. These lanterns go on the low hooks.' Beatriz stood on a stool, Mamãe holding her waist, and hung six red lanterns one by one, counting in Portuguese. One hung crooked. Mr. Chen left it. All week Beatriz pointed out 'my lanterns' to every customer, and she circled the date on the kitchen calendar with a red crayon.

qa.q: How many lanterns did Beatriz hang?
qa.a: Six red lanterns.

qa.q: How did Beatriz feel about 'my lanterns' all week?
qa.a: She felt proud and excited, showing them to every customer as her own work.

qa.q: What made Mr. Chen's invitation meaningful for Beatriz?
qa.a: He called it an important job, gave her a real task at her height and left the crooked lantern, so it truly felt like hers.

qa.q: How might Mr. Chen's customers feel when Beatriz shows off her lanterns?
qa.a: They would likely feel charmed and drawn into the festival mood by her pride.

grounding: Illustrates a young child proud to be given a real task in preparing for a festival, which gives her a place in the community and a date to look forward to.

passage:
Monday: Dadi tells Pranav, nine, about Prahlad and Holika while they shape gujiyas. 'But why didn't the fire burn Prahlad?' Pranav asks. 'Because he held on to what was good,' Dadi says. Pranav frowns, thinking.
Wednesday: At school Pranav retells it to his friend Raghav, sound effects and all. Raghav says, 'At Onam we have a story too. King Mahabali comes home once a year to see if his people are happy.' 'Why only once?' 'Ask my Achan.'
Saturday: At Holi, Pranav smears green on Raghav's cheek and whispers, 'Next Onam, you tell me the whole thing. Deal?'

qa.q: What were Dadi and Pranav shaping?
qa.a: Gujiyas.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he frowned after Dadi's answer?
qa.a: He felt curious and a little puzzled, still thinking about why the fire didn't burn Prahlad.

qa.q: How could Dadi or Raghav's Achan keep the friends' questions going?
qa.a: Welcome the 'why' questions, tell the stories in full, and let the two friends share each other's festivals and ask more.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel when Pranav asks to hear the whole Onam story?
qa.a: Raghav would likely feel proud and happy that a friend values Raghav's festival too.

grounding: Shows a child who hears the story behind Holi, asks why, and comes away curious about both his own festival and his friend's.

passage: Gopika, you ask why your Ammamma Manjula makes payasam at Onam and also a plum cake at Christmas? Sit. When I was ten, in Kottayam, my own Ammamma told me about Mahabali every Onam while I arranged the flowers. I kept asking, 'But why did Vamana push a good king down?' She never scolded. She said, 'Good question. Keep asking.' That December my friend Mary's mother let me help stir the cake and told me about a baby born in a stable. I asked why a king would be born among cows. She laughed. 'Good question.' I went home with two stories that year, both full of whys. I still keep both.

qa.q: What did Mary's mother let young Manjula help with?
qa.a: Stir the cake.

qa.q: What was young Manjula feeling when she kept asking about Mahabali?
qa.a: She felt curious and a little troubled, wondering why a good king would be pushed down.

qa.q: Which choice by the adults in the story helped young Manjula most?
qa.a: Ammamma and Mary's mother welcomed her questions instead of scolding, so the stories became her own and her friend's festival mattered too.

qa.q: How might Mary's mother have felt when young Manjula asked about the stable?
qa.a: She seemed amused and pleased, laughing and calling it a good question, glad to share her festival.

grounding: Illustrates a child who hears the stories behind Onam and a friend's Christmas, asks why, and carries home a sense of both festivals.

passage: I'm Charu, Naveen's older sister. Three days before Diwali, Naveen had plans: cricket with friends, then a film. Instead Ma handed him a duster and the fan-cleaning job. He grumbled all morning, loud enough for the neighbours, and banged the ladder about. But when Nani began the story of the year the kitchen curtains caught a spark on Diwali, he stopped, sat on the ladder and laughed the hardest. At lunch he asked Ma, 'If I finish the fans and the balcony by four, can I have the evening?' Ma agreed. He finished at 3:45. I don't know what he was thinking, but he was humming by then.

qa.q: What time did Naveen finish?
qa.a: He finished at 3:45.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling while he grumbled and banged the ladder about?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and frustrated at losing his plans, though Nani's story soon pulled him back into the family fun.

qa.q: What was smart about Naveen's deal with Ma?
qa.a: He offered to finish specific jobs by a set time in exchange for his evening, so both the festival work and his own plans were respected.

qa.q: How did Charu see Naveen's mood change through the day?
qa.a: Charu noticed him go from loud grumbling to laughing at Nani's story to humming, though she couldn't be sure what he thought.

grounding: Shows a teenager pulled into festival cleaning while wanting time with friends, grumbling yet belonging, and asking for his own evening in return for sharing the work.

passage:
Tuesday: Ganpati arrives on Friday, and Mahima Kaku has a list. Tejas cleans the puja room, runs to the market twice, and strings the marigolds. Tejas, fifteen, had planned a gaming night with friends. He mutters, 'Why is it always me?'
Friday: Tejas stands in the crowded hall during the aarti, cymbals ringing, smelling the modaks he helped carry. Kaku catches his eye and mouths, 'Thank you.' He grins despite himself.
Sunday: After the immersion, he tells Kaku, 'I liked it. But next year can I have Saturday evening for my friends?' Kaku nods. 'Deal. And your cousin Omi takes the market runs.'

qa.q: What did Tejas have to string?
qa.a: The marigolds.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling during the aarti on Friday?
qa.a: He felt a warm sense of belonging and quiet pride, grinning when Kaku thanked him despite his earlier grumbling.

qa.q: How did Tejas and Kaku balance duty and personal time?
qa.a: Tejas asked calmly for one evening with friends, and Kaku agreed and shared the market runs with a cousin.

qa.q: How might Mahima Kaku feel hearing Tejas say he liked it?
qa.a: Kaku would likely feel happy and relieved, seeing that the work brought him closer to the family, not only resentment.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who grumbles about festival chores but also feels he belongs, and then asks for some personal time while the duty is shared.

passage:
All December, Yuki watched the windows on her street in Uppsala fill with candle-bridges and paper stars. Her family had moved from Osaka in August. At school everyone talked about Lucia morning and saffron buns, and Yuki nodded, understanding the words but not the feeling. Walking home, she counted lit windows; theirs was the only dark one.
On the thirteenth, Anders from next door knocked, holding a paper bag. 'My mum says come for Lucia breakfast. Your whole family. Bring nothing.' Yuki's mother bowed twice at the door. The next morning Yuki sat in a warm kitchen, a saffron bun in each hand, while Anders's little sister taught her the song.

qa.q: Where had Yuki's family moved from?
qa.a: From Osaka.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling as she counted lit windows on the way home?
qa.a: She felt lonely and left out, noticing that her home was the only dark window on the street.

qa.q: Why did Anders's invitation matter so much?
qa.a: It was simple and cost little, but it brought the whole family inside the festival instead of watching from outside.

qa.q: How might Anders's family have felt hosting Yuki's family for Lucia?
qa.a: They probably felt glad and warm, sharing their tradition and helping new neighbours feel at home.

grounding: Shows a teenager from a migrant family who feels outside the neighbours' festival until a simple invitation from next door brings her in.

passage:
In Class 9 at the Lucknow school, Diwali week meant rangoli contests, diya painting and talk of whose house would have the best lights. Sabina, fourteen, new since July, painted her diya carefully but ate lunch alone while the others planned visits. Her family was the only Christian one on their lane, and no one had knocked yet.
On Thursday, Nandini slid onto the bench beside her. 'Come to our place on Diwali evening? Ma makes the best kaju katli. And my Nani wants to meet the girl who painted that peacock diya.'
Sabina blinked. 'Really?'
'Really. Bring your brother too.'
For the first time that week, Sabina laughed out loud.

qa.q: What did Sabina paint on the diya?
qa.a: A peacock.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling while eating lunch alone during Diwali week?
qa.a: She felt lonely and outside, watching the others plan visits while her family had no invitations yet.

qa.q: What could other classmates learn from Nandini?
qa.a: That a simple, warm invitation to a new student costs little and can make a huge difference.

qa.q: How might Nandini's Nani feel meeting Sabina on Diwali?
qa.a: Nani would likely feel pleased and welcoming, eager to meet the girl whose diya impressed her.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager from a minority family who feels outside while classmates celebrate, and how a friend's invitation makes a large difference at little cost.

passage: Rehana, I can see you're homesick for Eid in this hostel. Let your Manoj Chacha tell you something. I was twenty, working my first job at a steel plant far from Varanasi, when Diwali came. I watched the lights of the colony from my room and felt as if someone had scooped out my chest. I thought about sleeping through it. Instead I cooked the one thing I knew, my mother's aloo sabzi, badly, and knocked on the door of Iqbal, the machine operator next door, who was also alone. We ate it off newspaper. Then I found a phone booth and called home. My mother cried. I cried. It still hurt, beta. But it hurt with company.

qa.q: What did young Manoj cook?
qa.a: His mother's aloo sabzi.

qa.q: What was young Manoj feeling as he watched the colony lights?
qa.a: He felt a sharp, aching homesickness, as if his chest had been scooped out.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped young Manoj most?
qa.a: Deciding not to sleep through Diwali but to cook one home dish, share it with Iqbal and call home, which eased the ache without pretending it was small.

qa.q: How might Iqbal have felt when Manoj knocked with the aloo sabzi?
qa.a: Iqbal, also alone, probably felt grateful and less lonely, sharing a festival meal off newspaper.

grounding: Shows a young worker far from home who feels a sharp ache at festival time and eases it by cooking one dish, sharing it and calling home, without pretending the loss is small.

passage: Onam fell on a Tuesday, and Gopika, twenty-one, had a double shift at the hospital canteen in Hyderabad where she worked while studying. Between orders, her family's photos kept arriving: Achan in a crisp mundu, the pookalam, the sadya on banana leaves. Her throat tightened each time. At 10 pm, with most shops shut and forty rupees in her wallet, she bought two bananas and a packet of jaggery. Dhruv, her co-worker, found her at the staff stove making a tiny sweet banana dish. 'What's this?' 'Onam, sort of.' She video-called home while it cooked, and Amma sang the Onam song. Dhruv ate half and asked about Mahabali. It wasn't home. But it wasn't nothing.

qa.q: What did Gopika buy at 10 pm?
qa.a: Two bananas and a packet of jaggery.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling as the family photos kept arriving?
qa.a: She felt a sharp ache of homesickness, her throat tightening each time.

qa.q: What helped Gopika cope with missing Onam?
qa.a: Cooking one small home dish, calling home while it cooked and sharing it with Dhruv, which eased the loss without pretending it was small.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have experienced this Onam at the canteen?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt curious and glad to be included, learning about Mahabali over half a sweet banana dish.

grounding: Illustrates a student far from home who sees the festival on a screen and feels a sharp ache, easing it with one home dish, a call and a friend's company.
